title: Perform primary meat inspection incisions of crocodile

lessons.title: Crocodile slaughter and preparing for inspection
lessons.html:
Background

Nile crocodiles are farmed in South Africa, mainly in Limpopo, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal. They are raised mainly for their skins, which are sold to the luxury leather trade, and the meat is a valuable by-product sold locally and for export. Crocodile meat must be slaughtered at a registered facility and inspected under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations.

Special hazards of crocodile meat

  • Salmonella and other bacteria are commonly carried by reptiles. Contamination from the gut and the skin is a major risk.
  • Parasites: Trichinella parasites have been found in farmed Nile crocodiles in southern Africa, so laboratory testing of muscle samples may be required by the regulations or by importing countries.
  • Other parasites, such as worms in the gut and lungs and pentastomids, may be found in organs.

Worker safety

Crocodiles are dangerous even after stunning and killing: jaw and tail reflexes can still cause injury. Follow the facility's procedure for securing the jaws and confirming death. Never place hands near the jaws until the animal is confirmed dead and the jaws are secured.

Preparing the station

  • Good lighting and a clean inspection table or rail.
  • A system that keeps organs matched to each carcass number.
  • Sterilizer, hand-wash basin, two sharp knives, steel, hook.
  • Sample containers and labels if Trichinella or other testing is required.
  • Detention area, tags and condemned containers.
  • PPE, including gloves where required, because of the high Salmonella risk.

Planning

Review the ante-mortem record: thin animals, animals with wounds from fighting, skin lesions, or animals that were not feeding. Confirm sampling requirements before slaughter starts.

lessons.title: Performing the inspection of crocodile
lessons.html:
Routine examination

Carry out the examination in the sequence prescribed by the regulations and your training. Because the skin is the main product, skinning is done with great care and the carcass is presented skinned for inspection.

Carcass

  • Observe the whole carcass, especially the tail and body wall muscles, which are the main meat cuts.
  • Look for bruising, bite wounds from fighting, abscesses, haemorrhages, oedema and emaciation. Emaciated crocodiles have wasted tail muscle and reduced fat bodies.
  • Check for contamination from the skin and from gut contents.
  • Incise muscle where lesions are suspected.
  • Take muscle samples for laboratory testing as required, labelled with the carcass number.

Organs

  • Lungs: observe and palpate for consolidation, nodules, abscesses and parasites.
  • Heart: observe the heart sac and heart surface for inflammation and haemorrhage.
  • Liver: observe and palpate both surfaces; incise where lesions are seen. Look for abscesses, nodules, discolouration and enlargement.
  • Spleen and kidneys: observe for enlargement and haemorrhage.
  • Digestive tract: observe the stomach and intestines. Crocodile stomachs often contain stones; look for foreign bodies, ulcers and parasites. Do not cut into the gut.

Hygiene

  • Sterilise knives after every carcass and immediately after cutting a lesion.
  • Wash hands often; reptile Salmonella spreads easily from hands and surfaces.
  • Keep the meat away from the skin side and gut contents.

lessons.title: Completing the crocodile inspection
lessons.html:
Findings and actions

FindingAction
No abnormalitiesHold pending laboratory results if testing is required; otherwise continue to marking
Localised bite wound or abscessMark for trimming
Parasites in one organCondemn affected organ; carcass continues if normal
Generalised oedema, emaciation or multiple abscessesDetain and refer; total condemnation likely
Gut contamination of meatTrim; if extensive, detain and refer
Positive Trichinella resultCondemn or treat strictly as the regulations and veterinarian direct

Holding carcasses for test results

When laboratory tests are required, carcasses must be held under control, identified by number, and not released until results are received and recorded. A system must ensure that samples and carcasses can be matched exactly.

Records

  • Carcass and skin numbers, farm of origin.
  • Findings, trimming, condemnations and detentions.
  • Samples taken, laboratory results and dates.

Feedback to the farm

Fighting wounds suggest overcrowding or mixing of sizes; emaciation suggests feeding or temperature problems; parasite findings point to feed or water sources. Feedback helps improve both skin and meat quality.

Safety reminder

Report any bite or scratch injury. Wounds from crocodiles and contaminated knives can become seriously infected. Get first aid and medical care.

Key points

  • Crocodiles are farmed mainly for skin, but the meat must be inspected under the Meat Safety Act.
  • Salmonella and Trichinella are important hazards in crocodile meat.
  • Secure the jaws and confirm death before handling the head.
  • Take and label samples carefully and hold carcasses until results are received.
  • Sterilise knives and wash hands often to control Salmonella.
